title: Camp 3 close: the practice is yours
hookLine: sixty days of tools; next, a poet and an emperor

lines: SIXTY DAYS AGO: I CAN DO THIS.
cards: Sixty days ago, this camp started with a promise in four words: I can do this. Not I understand this, or I've read about this. Do.
Back then, practice might have sounded like something other people did: monks, athletes, people with more time. Look at what you've done since. You've watched ten breaths and sighed on purpose.
You've previewed mornings and reviewed evenings. You've sorted worries into mine and not mine, counted good things, looked down from a mile up, and remembered you will die.
You've walked, scanned, slept, served, hidden your phone and watched the sun go. Today, the camp's last day, it comes together.

teach.b: Here's the whole camp, in order. Week one: breath, from just watching to box breathing. Week two: bookends, Marcus's morning preview and Seneca's evening review.
Week three: the dichotomy of control, Epictetus's two columns. Week four: gratitude, three good things and grace before meals.
Week five: the view from above, the pale blue dot, memento mori and the Buddha's five remembrances. Week six: walking, kayagatasati and sleep. Week seven: service, one act a week.
Week eight: the digital sabbath, borrowed with respect from Shabbat. Week nine: sunset as a ritual. And this last week: your five, their smallest versions, and starting again.
The Stoics had a word for all this: askesis, training, the way an athlete trains. Epictetus taught that philosophy isn't only for reading; it's exercise, done daily, in small reps.
Dictionaries trace the English word ascetic to the same Greek root, but the older sense is simpler: practice. That's what this camp was.

Not beliefs to adopt; nobody on this path has told you what to believe. Tools, borrowed carefully from traditions and from science, each named, each left in its own home. What you do with them is yours.

teach.h: NEXT: A POET AND AN EMPEROR.
teach.b: The next camp reads a text slowly: two books, side by side.
One by a thirteenth-century Persian poet, a Muslim scholar named Jalal al-Din Rumi. One by a second-century Roman emperor writing private notes to himself: Marcus Aurelius, whom you've already met.

how: People who keep a personal spiritual practice outside a single tradition often settle on a short daily routine of a few practices, such as breath, a morning intention, an evening review and a walk, and adjust it over time.

o: a Greek word for quiet prayer inside a monastery
the Greek name for a monk's plain woolen robe
training: daily practice, the way an athlete trains

games.q: which week, which practice — tap the pairs.

s: askesis originally meant training, like an athlete's
the Stoics used it for daily practice; English 'ascetic' comes from it later.
this camp asked you to adopt a set of beliefs
tools, not beliefs: each borrowed carefully and left in its own home.
the next camp reads Rumi and Marcus Aurelius side by side
a Persian poet and a Roman emperor: two voices, never merged.

games.q: the camp is over. you have five practices and their smallest versions. what now?
o: put the list away; the camp is done.
games.why: keep doing them, your way. askesis means training, and training is daily, in small reps.

practice: Do your whole routine once, in its smallest form: one breath's worth of your first practice, then the second, third, fourth and fifth, picturing a walk or a sunset for a breath.
Then rest, and feel it: your whole routine fit inside two minutes. Say inside: I can do this.

wordCard.voice: Askesis, the Greek word for training, the exercise-like daily practice the Stoics believed philosophy required. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, askesis: training, exercise. the Stoics used it for daily practice; English 'ascetic' comes from it.

carryVoice: Your line: I can do this. Full size or smallest size, both count. Camp three, complete.
